lead: Support protocols let a host use IP. ARP finds the MAC for a local IPv4 address. ICMP reports errors and tests reachability. DHCP gives a host its IP configuration. NAT lets many private hosts share one public address. Together they make everyday Internet work.
prereq: You need: IPv4 addressing, Subnetting, and IPv4 datagram basics.

blocks.text: ARP stands for Address Resolution Protocol. It works in IPv4 networks over Ethernet and other broadcast link layers such as Wi‑Fi. It is not limited to Ethernet.
A host that wants to send an IP packet must know the destination MAC address on the same LAN.

items: Host creates an ARP request. The request broadcast address is ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff.
The request contains the sender IP, sender MAC, target IP, and a zero target MAC.
All hosts on the LAN receive the request.
The host whose IP matches the target IP replies with an ARP reply that includes its MAC.

blocks.text: The ARP reply is a unicast Ethernet frame addressed to the requester’s MAC.
ICMP stands for Internet Control Message Protocol. It lives inside the IP payload.
The most common ICMP message is the echo request and echo reply used by the ping utility.

items: Host A sends an IP packet with protocol = 1 (ICMP) and type = 8 (echo request).
If Host A and Host B are on different networks, the router forwards the packet; otherwise the packet is delivered directly on the LAN.
Host B receives the request, changes type to 0 (echo reply), and swaps source and destination IPs.
Host B sends the reply back to Host A.

blocks.text: ICMP also carries error messages such as Destination Unreachable and Time Exceeded.
When a router cannot forward a packet, it creates an ICMP Destination Unreachable message and sends it to the source.
IPv6 does not use ARP. It uses Neighbor Discovery, which is carried in ICMPv6 messages.
DHCP stands for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. It automates IP address allocation.
A DHCP client uses UDP ports 68 (client) and 67 (server).

items: Client broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER. The message contains a transaction ID and a MAC address.
DHCP server replies with DHCPOFFER. The offer includes an IP address, subnet mask, router, DNS, lease time, and the same transaction ID.
Client sends DHCPREQUEST to accept the offer. It repeats the transaction ID and the offered IP.
Server sends DHCPACK confirming the lease and repeats the configuration parameters.

blocks.text: If the client does not receive a DHCPOFFER, it retransmits DHCPDISCOVER after a timeout.
The lease time tells the client how long it may use the address before renewing.
DHCP can also provide options such as NTP server or custom vendor data.
In a home Wi‑Fi router, the DHCP server typically hands out addresses in the 192.168.0.0/24 range.

sections.h3: NAT source‑port translation and practical notes

blocks.text: NAT stands for Network Address Translation. It lets many private hosts share a single public IP.
The most common form is source‑port NAT (also called PAT).

items: A private host (192.168.0.50) creates a TCP segment with source port 54321 and destination port 80.
Router rewrites the source IP to its public address (203.0.113.20) and may also change the source port to a unique value, e.g., 40000.
Router stores a table entry mapping (public IP, public port) → (private IP, private port).
When a reply arrives, the router looks up the table, restores the original private IP and port, and forwards the packet.

blocks.text: Only the source port is changed in typical home NAT. The destination port stays as the server expects.
NAT breaks end‑to‑end connectivity for protocols that embed IP addresses in the payload, such as SIP or FTP.
In IPv6, NAT is rarely needed because the address space is large enough for every device to have a globally routable address.

examples.question: A laptop connects to a home Wi‑Fi router. It receives IP 192.168.0.50 via DHCP. The router’s MAC is 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. The laptop sends an ICMP echo request to google.com (IP 172.217.3.110). The router translates the source to public IP 203.0.113.20 and source port 54321 using NAT. List the four DHCP messages, the ARP request and reply, and the final NAT‑translated source address and port.
steps: DHCPREQUEST from laptop accepting the offer.
DHCPACK from router confirming the lease.
ICMP echo request leaves laptop with src IP 192.168.0.50, src port N/A (ICMP).
Router rewrites src IP to 203.0.113.20 and src port to 54321 (PAT).
examples.answer: The DHCP messages are DHCPDISCOVER, DHCPOFFER, DHCPREQUEST, DHCPACK. ARP request and ARP reply occur as shown. NAT changes the source to 203.0.113.20:54321.
examples.check:
import sys
# No input needed
public_ip_last_octet = 20
source_port = 54321
print(public_ip_last_octet)
print(source_port)

traps: Assuming NAT always changes the destination port; only the source port (or address) is altered in typical home PAT.
Confusing the ARP request target IP (gateway) with the IP being assigned by DHCP; they are different addresses.
Treating ICMP as a transport‑layer protocol; it is an IP‑layer control message and has no ports.
Believing that IPv6 uses ARP; IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery instead.

quiz.q: Why does a DHCP client broadcast DHCPDISCOVER?
quiz.a: Because the client does not yet have an IP address or a known DHCP server, so it must reach all servers on the local network.

quiz.q: A host with MAC AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF sends an ARP request for IP 192.168.1.10. The reply contains MAC 11:22:33:44:55:66. What MAC will the host use for the next packet to 192.168.1.10?
quiz.a: The host will use MAC 11:22:33:44:55:66 as the destination Ethernet address.

quiz.q: A router receives a TCP SYN from 192.168.0.20:40000 to 93.184.216.34:80. Its public IP is 203.0.113.5. It translates the source port to 55000. What source address and port appear on the internet?
If a host sends an ICMP Destination Unreachable message, what part of the original packet is included in the ICMP payload?
quiz.a: The IP header and the first 8 bytes of the original payload, enough to identify the original flow.

quiz.q: Which UDP ports are used by DHCP client and server?
quiz.a: Client uses port 68, server uses port 67.

quiz.q: Explain why NAT breaks end‑to‑end connectivity for FTP active mode.
quiz.a: FTP active mode tells the server to connect back to the client’s IP and port. NAT rewrites the client’s IP, so the server’s connection attempt reaches the NAT device, not the client, causing failure.

quiz.q: Compare the role of ICMP in IPv4 and IPv6.
quiz.a: In IPv4, ICMP carries error messages and echo requests/replies. In IPv6, the same functions are provided by ICMPv6, which also includes Neighbor Discovery messages that replace ARP.

beyond: Not for the exam. In modern data‑center networks, ARP tables are offloaded to switches to reduce broadcast traffic. Cloud providers use DHCPv6 and SLAAC together for flexible IPv6 address assignment. Researchers explore stateful NAT64 to enable IPv6‑only clients to reach IPv4 services. Look for "software‑defined networking" and "edge NAT" for the next steps.
